michael-dell.reviewDepth: Source-led review of stated episodes; broader coverage still limited
michael-dell.period: Trump Accounts pledge, December 2025; software procurement, May 2026
michael-dell.summary: Dell’s support for a presidential savings initiative sits alongside a major government software agreement. This warrants scrutiny, but the reviewed procurement account supplies an ordinary purchasing rationale rather than evidence of a personal exchange.
michael-dell.mechanism: Public philanthropy and government procurement; causal connection unproven

support.text: Michael and Susan Dell pledged $6.25 billion toward children’s investment accounts using the Trump Accounts program. The announced beneficiaries were children, not the president personally.
support.access: Indexed source passage reviewed; article retrieval unavailable

support.text: The Pentagon awarded Dell Federal Systems a five-year software-purchasing agreement valued at about $9.7 billion. It consolidated existing budgets rather than creating that amount of new funding.

counter.text: Officials described procurement consolidation and projected annual savings. A company contract is not evidence that Michael Dell personally traded his philanthropy for preferential treatment.

michael-dell.limitations: This is an episode-specific estimate, not a finding about procurement legality. Contract face value is neither Dell profit nor a personal payment. Broader political activity and award-selection records remain outside this review.

miriam-adelson.reviewDepth: Source-led review of stated episodes; broader coverage still limited
miriam-adelson.summary: Adelson’s Texas political financing pursues a clear commercial-policy objective. The reviewed campaign also shows substantial limits: spending did not deliver the desired legalization.
miriam-adelson.mechanism: Casino wealth → electoral financing → attempted market-opening policy

support.text: The Tribune reports Adelson financing casino-aligned PACs and a broad set of legislative campaigns. In November 2025, the casino-backed Senate candidate failed to reach the runoff.
March 2026 reporting records further defeats for casino-backed challengers and continuing legislative resistance. Sands defended supporting candidates who favor a business-friendly economy.

counter.text: Several anti-gambling candidates won despite opposing spending. Legalization also requires voter approval of a constitutional amendment: donor financing is not unilateral control.

miriam-adelson.limitations: The estimate covers this attempted economic-policy influence, not all US or Israeli activity. Miriam’s actions are separated from her late husband’s. Lawful advocacy is not bribery; an unsuccessful campaign is not a received concession.

stephen-schwarzman.reviewDepth: Source-led review of stated episodes; broader coverage still limited
stephen-schwarzman.summary: Schwarzman’s high-level political access and private-equity tax interests form a documented influence channel. The evidence is stronger for coordinated industry lobbying than for a personal quid pro quo.
stephen-schwarzman.mechanism: Political access and industry lobbying ↔ preservation of favorable tax treatment

support.text: CNN reported Schwarzman hosting a Trump fundraiser and helping form the president’s business advisory council. It connected the carried-interest debate to his financial interests.

The Journal describes Blackstone’s participation in the industry lobbying coalition and preservation of carried-interest treatment in 2022. It cites securities filings showing Schwarzman received substantial carry and incentive compensation.
support.source: The Wall Street Journal via Mint

counter.text: Blackstone told CNN the overall 2017 bill would increase Schwarzman’s personal taxes because of other provisions. That differs from the narrower benefit of retaining carried-interest treatment.
The industry and Senator Sinema offered investment and growth reasons for the tax treatment. Many firms shared the benefit; the reporting does not prove Schwarzman personally determined the vote.
counter.source: The Wall Street Journal via Mint: competing rationale

stephen-schwarzman.limitations: This historical estimate does not assert the current tax code or a corruption finding. Industry coordination, individual access and financial exposure are distinguishable; legislative causation remains contested.

thomas-peterffy.reviewDepth: Source-led review of stated episodes; broader coverage still limited
thomas-peterffy.summary: The reviewed donor episode demonstrates political participation and willingness to withhold support. It does not establish the business benefit needed for a defensible oligarchy estimate.
thomas-peterffy.mechanism: Donor leverage; preferential economic exchange unresolved

support.text: Reporting describes Peterffy putting prospective DeSantis support on hold, citing abortion and school-book policies. This identifies stated policy preferences, not a business concession.
support.source: The Washington Post via Portland Press Herald

counter.text: The same account presents disagreement between a donor and a politician. Withholding support does not show the politician obeyed, or that the donor received a private economic return.

thomas-peterffy.limitations: No numeric score is assigned from campaign giving alone. Land, taxation and brokerage regulation require separate person-specific research; neither clearance nor wrongdoing is inferred from this narrow review.

german-larrea-mota-velasco.reviewDepth: Source-led review of stated episodes; broader coverage still limited
german-larrea-mota-velasco.summary: The Ferrosur episode documents a state–company negotiation, but the concession change was compensation following state occupation. Treating that alone as a gift to Larrea would omit the loss on the other side of the transaction.
german-larrea-mota-velasco.mechanism: Railway concession renegotiation following government occupation

support.text: Reuters reported an agreement to extend expiring concessions rather than pay cash after government forces occupied a railway section controlled by Grupo México’s transport business.
Earlier Reuters reporting records the president proposing concession restructuring as compensation after the takeover. It does not establish Larrea’s personal control over the state.

counter.text: The occupation itself and non-cash compensation are material constraints on the patronage interpretation. The transaction cannot be evaluated as a benefit without valuing what the company surrendered.

german-larrea-mota-velasco.limitations: No score: concession value, individual negotiating role and broader privatization history remain unresolved. Company and family assets are not automatically evidence of personal political favoritism.

masayoshi-son.reviewDepth: Source-led review of stated episodes; broader coverage still limited
masayoshi-son.summary: Son’s Stargate role combines a very large investment ambition with presidential-stage access. The announcement is not evidence that the US government supplied the headline capital or granted Son a preferential private benefit.
masayoshi-son.mechanism: Investment pledge and political promotion; specific preferential return unresolved

support.text: Son appeared with Trump at Stargate’s announcement.
SoftBank’s announcement names Son as chairman, identifies the initial equity funders and assigns financial responsibility to SoftBank. The $500 billion figure is an intended four-year investment.

counter.text: The company identifies equity investors, not a $500 billion US appropriation, and warns that forward-looking plans may differ from outcomes. An announcement is not completed spending.

masayoshi-son.limitations: No score is assigned from an investment pledge and access alone. Actual incentives, financing terms, regulatory decisions and other countries require separate review; this is not a whole-career assessment.

rationales: Visible support for a presidential policy initiative.
Government sales are documented; exceptional preferential terms are not established here.
The timing warrants questions but does not establish a reciprocal favor.
Sustained electoral financing directed toward a commercial-policy goal.
The reviewed Texas campaign had not delivered legalization; zero applies to this episode, not her entire business history.
A clear attempted wealth–policy link, constrained by electoral and legislative defeats.
Direct presidential access and fundraising are documented.
A favorable industry-wide tax provision benefits his compensation class.
Organized lobbying and preserved benefits support an influence inference, not proof of a personal bargain.
